Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

School & learning

subtract verb

also take away, subtraction, minus

classical

Varr. LL 5.172: ūnā dēmptā ūnciā deūnx (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Ac. 2.49: quom aliquid minūtātim et gradātim additur aut dēmitur

dēmō, dēmere, dēmpsī, dēmptum

verb, third conjugation

take away, subtract

Varro explains the names of the fractions by it: eleven twelfths, deūnx, is the whole with one twelfth taken away. From a total, dē summā dēmere.

Examples

  • sī dē quīncūnce remōta est ūncia, quid superat? … — triēns. — eu! rem poteris servāre tuam. redit ūncia, quid fit? — sēmis

    If one twelfth is taken from five twelfths, what is left? — A third. — Well done! You’ll be able to look after your money. Put the twelfth back: what does it make? — A half.Hor. Ars 327–330

Other words

  • dēdūcō, dēdūcere, dēdūxī, dēductum — deduct

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 1.59: addendō dēdūcendōque; Liv. 6.15.10: dē capite dēdūcite, quod ūsūrīs pernumerātum est

    The accountant’s word: deduct from the capital what has been paid in interest (Liv. 6.15.10).

  • dētrahō, dētrahere, dētrāxī, dētractum — take away (from a total)

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Traupman 32

    Classically to draw off, take away; aliquid dē summā dētrahere (Lewis & Short). Traupman’s word for subtract.

  • subtrahō, subtrahere, subtrāxī, subtractum — subtract

    verb, third conjugation · also used · Renaissance · Comen. OP 101: addendō, subtrahendō, multiplicandō, dīvidendō

    Classically to draw away from under, to withdraw (Lewis & Short); the arithmetic sense is not classical, but later arithmetic used it, and English takes subtract from it.

See also sum, arithmetic, add, multiply, divide.
